stances.claim: Our criminal justice system is overprotective of the guilty because it passionately safeguards individual life and liberty, adhering to the maxim better to acquit 10 guilty than convict 1 innocent -- but the ratio sometimes worsens to 100:1 or 1000:1 when corruption, negligence, incompetence, or outright malevolence seeps in.

Our judiciary strictly adheres to the adversarial system (passive magistrates, cold neutrality, referees not players, three-evidence-source rule) while our prosecutorial agencies (OOO, DOJ, city/provincial prosecutors) use the inquisitorial method -- this split-system is itself part of the problem.

Prosecutors are authorized by law to file criminal charges including capital offenses based only on probable cause, but to secure conviction they must reach proof-beyond-reasonable-doubt -- this standards gap means that if all prosecutors prove at trial is probable cause, the accused will surely be acquitted, explaining low conviction rates.

Is it not unfair to accused who face capital offenses and indefinite detention pending trial only to be acquitted for insufficient evidence -- and a waste of state resources? Prosecutors should make sure they have enough evidence to convict before filing criminal cases, especially capital offenses.

The judge-must-inhibit-and-take-the-stand rule for personally-witnessed events -- converted from judge to ordinary witness subject to cross-examination -- a procedural detail rarely surfaced even by lawyer-readers.

The Field Investigation Office (FIO) as OOO internal-complainant explained -- served as complainant in the GMA plunder case dismissed by Morales last week (A414 cross-reference) -- illustrates the OOO's self-starting investigative capacity.
The ratio-worsening caveat (10:1 → 100:1 → 1000:1) -- a rare moment where CJP openly acknowledges that the noble adversarial maxim degrades catastrophically when systemic corruption sets in.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban responds to weekly reader questions about why our criminal justice system is overprotective of the guilty -- why it takes so long to investigate, prosecute, and convict, why conviction rates remain dismal -- with a structural diagnosis. He begins with the foundational maxim 'better to acquit 10 guilty than convict 1 innocent,' adding the bleak caveat that the ratio worsens to 100:1 or 1,000:1 when corruption, negligence, incompetence, or outright malevolence seeps in. The judiciary strictly adheres to the adversarial system -- passive magistrates sitting with the cold neutrality of an impartial judge, acting like referees not players in a basketball game, restricted to three evidence sources (facts proven by parties per the law on evidence, admissions/confessions, judicial notice), forbidden to convict or acquit based on personal knowledge (which would require inhibition and a turn as ordinary witness subject to cross-examination). By contrast, the prosecutorial agencies -- OOO, DOJ, city/provincial prosecutors -- use the inquisitorial method, mandated to help victims of crimes, free to call PNP/NBI assistance, with the OOO's Field Investigation Office serving even as internal-complainant (as in the GMA plunder case Morales dismissed last week). The structural problem he identifies: prosecutors may file criminal charges including capital offenses on mere probable cause (existence of facts and circumstances as would excite belief in a reasonable mind that respondent is guilty), but must secure proof-beyond-reasonable-doubt for conviction -- and if all they can prove at trial is probable cause, the accused will surely be acquitted, explaining low conviction rates. He poses rhetorical questions: Is this not unfair to capital-offense accused detained indefinitely only to be acquitted for insufficient evidence -- and a waste of state resources? Should not prosecutors make sure they have enough evidence to convict before filing, especially capital offenses? He promises to continue in future columns on the due-process concept that is sometimes abused and misused to miscarry justice.
